function getParameterByName(name, url) {
		if(url == null){
		  url = window.location.href;
		}
	    name = name.replace(/[\[\]]/g, '\\$&');
	    var regex = new RegExp('[?&]' + name + '(=([^&#]*)|&|#|$)'),
		results = regex.exec(url);
	    if (!results) return null;
	    if (!results[2]) return '';
	    return decodeURIComponent(results[2].replace(/\+/g, ' '));
	}

    var STYLE_ID = 'at-body-style';
    function getParent() {
    return doc.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
    }
    function addStyle(parent, id, def) {
        if (!parent) {
        return;
        }
        var style = doc.createElement('style');
        style.id = id;
        style.innerHTML = def;
        parent.appendChild(style);
    }
    function removeStyle(parent, id) {
        if (!parent) {
            return;
        }
        var style = doc.getElementById(id);
        if (!style) {
            return;
        }
        parent.removeChild(style);
    }
    addStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID, style);
    setTimeout(function() {
    removeStyle(getParent(), STYLE_ID);
    }, timeout);

 * String.prototype.replaceAll() polyfill

 * @author Chris Ferdinandi
 * @license MIT

if (!String.prototype.replaceAll) {
	String.prototype.replaceAll = function(str, newStr){
		// If a regex pattern
		if (Object.prototype.toString.call(str).toLowerCase() === '[object regexp]') {
			return this.replace(str, newStr);
		}
		// If a string
		return this.replace(new RegExp(str, 'g'), newStr);
	};

	function getCookie(cname) {
	 	var name = cname + "=";
  		var decodedCookie = decodeURIComponent(document.cookie);
		var ca = decodedCookie.split(';');
  		for(var i = 0; i <ca.length; i++) {
    			var c = ca[i];
    			while (c.charAt(0) == ' ') {
     				 c = c.substring(1);
    			}
    			if (c.indexOf(name) == 0) {
    				 return c.substring(name.length, c.length);
    			}
  		}
  		return "";
	}

	var referer = "";//sessionStorage.container;

function callMainSitePrismaNavHTML(){
    
    var referrer_domain = 'https://www.paloaltonetworks.com';
    sessionStorage.setItem("domain",referrer_domain);
    if(referer == 'Prisma'){

        }
    if(referer == 'CloudCortex'){
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=cortexcloud&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexcloudsearch";	
    }

        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/cortexsearch";	
    }
    if(referer == 'Sase'){
        //var menu_url = referrer_domain+'/_jcr_content/globals/cleanHeaderSase.saseRenderer.html';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=sase&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/sasesearch";
    }
    if(referer == 'Unit'){
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=unit42&domain=en';
        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/content/pan/en_US/search/unit42search";
		    }
    if(referer == 'Ngfw'){

        searchResultsPagePath = referrer_domain+"/search/ngfwcdsssearch";

        //var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/ngfw-cdss-nav-renderer.php';
        var menu_url = 'https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/themes/unit42-v6/unit-nav-renderer.php?type=idira&domain=en';

    }
    httpGet(menu_url,'menu_html');

}
function addStyle(styles) {            
    /* Create style document */
    var css = document.createElement('style');
    css.type = 'text/css';

    if (css.styleSheet) 
        css.styleSheet.cssText = styles;
    else 
        css.appendChild(document.createTextNode(styles));

    /* Append style to the tag name */
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(css);
}
function httpGet(theUrl,req_type) {
    if (window.XMLHttpRequest) { // code for IE7+, Firefox, Chrome, Opera, Safari
        xmlhttp=new XMLHttpRequest();
    } else {// code for IE6, IE5
        xmlhttp=new ActiveXObject("Microsoft.XMLHTTP");
    }
    xmlhttp.onreadystatechange=function()
    {
        if (xmlhttp.readyState==4 && xmlhttp.status==200)
        {
            if(req_type == 'menu_html'){
            var nav_text = xmlhttp.responseText.replaceAll('https://static.cloud.coveo.com/searchui/v2.9159/js/CoveoJsSearch.Lazy.min.js', '');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll('src="/', 'src="'+maindomain_lang+'/');
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("src='/", "src='"+maindomain_lang+"/");
            nav_text = nav_text.replaceAll("'/content", "'"+maindomain_lang+"/content");
                        
            document.getElementById("PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC").innerHTML = nav_text.replaceAll('href="/', 'href="'+maindomain_lang+'/');

            var lozad_back = document.getElementsByClassName('lozad-background');
            Array.prototype.forEach.call(lozad_back, function(el) {
            // Do stuff here
            var el_back_img_path = el.getAttribute('data-background-image');
            var first_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'");
            var last_pos = el_back_img_path.indexOf("'",first_pos+1);
            el_back_img_path = el_back_img_path.substring(first_pos+1,last_pos);
            let result = el_back_img_path.includes(main_site_url);
            if(result == false){
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",main_site_url+el_back_img_path);
            }
            else{
                el.setAttribute("data-background-image",el_back_img_path);
            }
            });
            const observer_lozad = lozad('.lozad, .lozad-background'); // lazy loads elements with default selector as '.lozad'
            observer_lozad.observe();
            }
            if(req_type == 'head_inline_css'){
            addStyle(xmlhttp.responseText);
            }
        }
    }
    xmlhttp.open("GET", theUrl, true );
    xmlhttp.send();    
}    
    
if(referer == 'Prisma' || referer == 'CloudCortex' || referer == 'Cortex' || referer == 'Sase' || referer == 'Unit' || referer == 'Ngfw' || referer == 'Idira'){

    }
    else if(referer == 'Sase'){
        article.dataset.type = 'sase';

    else if(referer == 'Unit'){
        article.dataset.type = 'unit';
    }
    else if(referer == 'Ngfw'){
        article.dataset.type = 'ngfw';

        $('#PAN_2021_NAV_ASYNC').removeClass('default').addClass('defaultRedesigned');

              <div class="be__contents-wrapper">
                <h2><a id="post-182090-_4lt92rr5muov"></a>Executive Summary</h2>
<p>Cloud logging services provide comprehensive visibility into actions performed within cloud resources, making them essential for security monitoring. However, this reliance also makes logging services a high-value target for attackers. An attacker who exploits these services could create weak spots, evade detection, and in certain scenarios, establish continuous visibility within a target’s environment.</p>
<p>Services such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) CloudTrail and Google Cloud are powerful for defenders, and prime targets for attackers seeking to remain undetected by disrupting the flow of logs. Attack techniques against cloud logging services primarily fall into two categories:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Defense Evasion:</strong> Attackers aim to bypass detection systems, to execute attacks unnoticed. This may involve modifying resources within the cloud logging service.</li>
<li><strong>Continuous Visibility:</strong> Attackers attempt to transfer logs to their own accounts, establishing continuous visibility over the victim's environment.</li>
</ul>
<p>Understanding these attack scenarios enables organizations to implement the appropriate configurations and detect service misuse.</p>
<p>Palo Alto Networks customers are better protected from the threats discussed above through the following products and services:</p>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/cortex/cloud" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cortex Cloud</a></li>
</ul>
<p>The <a href="https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/unit42/assess/cloud-security-assessment" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Cloud Security Assessment</a> is an evaluation service that reviews cloud infrastructure to identify misconfigurations and security gaps.</p>
<p>If you think you might have been compromised or have an urgent matter, contact the <a href="https://start.paloaltonetworks.com/contact-unit42.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Unit 42 Incident Response team</a>.</p>
<table style="width: 100%;">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="width: 35%;"><b>Related Unit 42 Topics</b></td>

</tr>

</table>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_16x3lsrwb948"></a>Cloud Logging Services</h2>
<p>Serving as the authoritative system of record for every event, cloud logging services provide complete visibility into all actions within cloud environments. This comprehensive data enables analysis of past behaviors for both operational debugging and security investigations.</p>
<p>Each cloud provider implements logging services in a unique way. Our recent <a href="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cloud-logging-for-security/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cloud Logging for Security</a> article provides an overview of these various services across different cloud providers. In this article, we analyze and demonstrate attack techniques that target the primary logging services within each major cloud provider.</p>
<p>Before examining the logging capabilities offered by major cloud providers, we outline the fundamental components and mechanisms for log delivery. Our analysis focuses on AWS CloudTrail and Google Cloud Logging. Both of these widely used services are designed to provide comprehensive audit trails and operational insights. While this article focuses on specific services, the attack techniques presented may also apply to other cloud logging services.</p>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_xsrr9k5n1hm6"></a>Background: How Cloud Service Providers Handle Logs</h2>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_5nm2wmqd3s2"></a>AWS CloudTrail</h3>
<p>AWS CloudTrail's primary resource for configurable log collection and delivery is known as a <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html#cloudtrail-concepts-trails" target="_blank" rel="noopener">trail</a>. A trail acts as a configuration that specifies how CloudTrail records AWS application programming interface (API) calls and related events in an AWS account. These events include actions taken by users, roles or AWS services.</p>
<p>The main function of a trail is to deliver these captured logs to an Amazon <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingBucket.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">S3 bucket</a>. S3 is a highly scalable, durable, secure object storage service. When a trail is configured, it continuously writes log files containing event records to the designated S3 bucket.</p>
<p>The S3 bucket serves as a centralized, long-term repository for CloudTrail logs. This enables auditing, security analysis and compliance efforts. CloudTrail supports sending native event trails to either the CloudTrail Lake feature, EventBridge or CloudWatch Logs. However, for enterprises with integrations to third-party products, these features might not be relevant or usable.</p>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_p7rghvhiit50"></a>Google Cloud Logging</h3>
<p>Cloud Logging is a fully managed service that collects logs from all of an organization’s Google Cloud resources. Cloud Logging leverages a resource called a <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/export/configure_export_v2" target="_blank" rel="noopener">sink</a> as the primary mechanism for log delivery. A sink functions as a router that sends log entries to a specific destination. While a sink primarily routes and stores logs in centralized <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets" target="_blank" rel="noopener">log buckets</a> for analysis and retention, it also offers the flexibility to export logs to other powerful Google Cloud services. For example, logs can be routed to a cloud storage bucket for cost-effective long-term archival. When a sink is configured, it exports log entries that match specific criteria defined by a filter to a designated log bucket.</p>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_3vsucvx3dzv1"></a>Defense Evasion</h2>
<p>Sophisticated techniques enable attackers to remain undetected within a compromised cloud environment. These methods could involve manipulating or evading logging mechanisms, which are crucial for security monitoring and incident response. Obscured activities can extend an attacker's presence, facilitate data exfiltration or inflict more harm before being discovered.</p>
<p>A wide array of security products including the following are fundamentally dependent on this log data to function:</p>
<ul>
<li>Security information and event management (SIEM)</li>
<li>Security orchestration, automation and response (SOAR) platforms</li>
<li>Specialized cloud security posture management (CSPM) tools</li>
</ul>
<p>By disabling, altering or deleting these logs, an attacker can effectively hide themselves from these defensive systems, compromising the security integrity of the entire cloud environment. Attackers often use the following five techniques to accomplish this:</p>
<ol>
<li>Stop logging</li>
<li>Delete the log storage destination</li>
<li>Delete the log router</li>
<li>Impair logging via attacker-controlled encryption key</li>
<li>Log poisoning</li>
</ol>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_ejl4rfyaplzy"></a>Technique 1: Stop Logging</h3>
<p>The most direct method to suspend log flows is to disable the logging mechanism itself. A wide array of security products is fundamentally dependent on this log data to function. By disabling these logs, an attacker can effectively blind defensive systems, compromising the security integrity of the entire cloud environment.</p>
<ul>
<li>In AWS, an attacker with <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">cloudtrail:StopLogging</span> permissions can invoke the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">stop-logging</span> API call for a specific trail. Once this API is executed, no further logs for that trail are written to the S3 bucket, creating an immediate visibility gap for organizations that created their own trails.</li>
<li>In Google Cloud, the equivalent action is disabling the sink. An attacker with <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">logging.sinks.update</span> permissions can set the sink’s <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">disabled</span> field to <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">true</span> to stop logs from being written. The Google Cloud console message shown in Figure 1 reflects this change.</li>
</ul>
<figure id="attachment_182091" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182091" style="width: 611px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182091 size-full lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-341857-182090-1.png" alt="A screenshot of a dialog box titled &quot;Confirm disable sink.&quot; It states the sink to be disabled is &quot;sink-blog-simulation.&quot; The message explains that disabling it will stop log export to this sink, and new logs will be lost unless captured by another sink. There are two buttons at the bottom: &quot;Cancel&quot; and &quot;Disable,&quot; with a link for more options on log sinks." width="611" height="310" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182091" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 1. Message confirming suspension of logs.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_gxepv2ed9cbg"></a>Technique 2: Delete Log Storage Destination</h3>
<p>Typically, logs are stored in a cloud storage resource. An attacker who obtains permission to this resource could delete the cloud storage, preventing logs from being written. The following scenarios demonstrate this ability.</p>
<ul>
<li>In AWS, an attacker with <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">s3:DeleteBucket</span> permissions can use the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">delete-bucket</span> API to delete the S3 bucket; this action also requires the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">s3:DeleteObject</span> permission to empty the bucket. A few minutes after the action, the associated CloudTrail trail's configuration will indicate this deletion, as the notification in Figure 2 shows.</li>
</ul>
<figure id="attachment_182102" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182102" style="width: 289px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182102 size-full lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-343694-182090-2.png" alt="A screenshot of a AWS CloudTrail displaying general details for a trail logging configuration. A red error message states &quot;Bucket doesn't exist&quot; with a &quot;Fix policy&quot; link. &quot;Multi-region trail&quot; is set to Yes, while &quot;Apply trail to my organization&quot; is Not Enabled." width="289" height="323" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182102" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 2. An indication for the bucket deletion in AWS CloudTrail.</figcaption></figure>
<ul>
<li>In Google Cloud, an attacker with <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">logging.buckets.delete</span> permissions can delete the log bucket. In the case of a log bucket, the deletion is not immediate. Once the delete command is issued, the log bucket enters a <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DELETE_REQUESTED</span> state, remaining in that state for seven days. After this period, the bucket is deleted.<br />
Google Cloud offers a <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/buckets#locking-logs-buckets" target="_blank" rel="noopener">mechanism</a> to protect against this deletion by providing the ability to lock the logging bucket. Once a bucket is locked, its retention policy becomes permanent and irreversible, meaning the bucket cannot be deleted by any user until every log entry within it has fulfilled the specified retention period.</li>
</ul>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_l19udt9xz237"></a>Technique 3: Delete Log Router</h3>
<p>Another defense evasion tactic involves deleting the log routing resource – for example, an AWS trail or a Google Cloud sink. Once deleted, new logs will cease to be written to the designated destination. An attacker can delete a log router by using the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">delete-trail</span> AWS API or the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">google.logging.v2.ConfigServiceV2.DeleteSink</span> Google Cloud method.</p>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_3v52pjzi1ldz"></a>Technique 4: Impair Logging via Attacker-Controlled Encryption Key</h3>
<p>​​An attacker could potentially render cloud logs unreadable by modifying their encryption key. An attack flow using AWS could unfold as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li>When a trail is created in AWS, one of the configuration parameters is the key management service (KMS) key, which is used to encrypt the logs delivered by CloudTrail.</li>
<li>An attacker could prevent legitimate access to this key by updating the trail to use an attacker-controlled KMS key and then removing access to the key.</li>
<li>Consequently, logs will not be written to the bucket due to the inability to encrypt them with the unusable key.</li>
<li>To perform this attack, an attacker first creates an external KMS key with the policy shown in Figure 3 to ensure that the key is accessible to CloudTrail.</li>
</ul>
<figure id="attachment_182113" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182113" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182113 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-345545-182090-3.png" alt="A code snippet showing a JSON policy configuration for AWS. The configuration permits CloudTrail access to a key." width="1000" height="544" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-345545-182090-3.png 1084w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-345545-182090-3-786x428.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-345545-182090-3-768x418.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182113" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 3. Policy to create a KMS key with external access.</figcaption></figure>
<ul>
<li>The attacker uses the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">update-trail</span> API to modify the KMS key used to encrypt the logs in the S3 bucket.</li>
<li>Next, the attacker removes CloudTrail's access to the key by either deleting the key or removing the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">Allow CloudTrail to access the key</span> statement from the policy. Subsequently, CloudTrail will indicate that there is a configuration issue due to denied bucket access, even though the bucket is correctly configured.</li>
<li>From this point on, logs will not be written to the bucket because the KMS key will be inaccessible. Figure 4 shows the message that is displayed after access is disabled.</li>
</ul>
<figure id="attachment_182124" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182124" style="width: 482px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182124 size-full lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-347506-182090-4.png" alt="A screenshot of AWS settings page displaying &quot;General details.&quot; It shows &quot;Trail logging&quot; with a red icon and the message &quot;Bucket access denied&quot; with a link to &quot;Fix policy.&quot; &quot;Multi-region trail&quot; is set to Yes, while &quot;Apply trail to my organization&quot; is Not Enabled." width="482" height="533" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-347506-182090-4.png 482w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-347506-182090-4-398x440.png 398w" sizes="(max-width: 482px) 100vw, 482px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182124" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 4. Disabling access to the KMS key results in a Bucket access denied error.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Figure 5 shows the attack flow using AWS.</p>
<figure id="attachment_182135" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182135" style="width: 785px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182135 size-full lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-349280-182090-5.png" alt="&quot;A diagram illustrating a three-step attack process on AWS CloudTrail. Step 1: Victim account stores logs in an S3 bucket, encrypted with its own KMS key. Step 2: Attacker uses 'update-trail' API to change the KMS key to one they control. Step 3: Attacker removes CloudTrail access to the original key, preventing victim access to logs." width="785" height="671" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-349280-182090-5.png 785w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-349280-182090-5-515x440.png 515w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-349280-182090-5-768x656.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 785px) 100vw, 785px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182135" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 5. Impair logging via attacker-controlled encryption key attack flow in AWS.</figcaption></figure>
<p>An attack flow using this technique in Google Cloud is as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li>In Google Cloud, a similar attack scenario can be simulated where a log bucket is already pre-configured with customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK). An attacker can then exploit this existing configuration by modifying the CMEK to reference an external key using the following command (the external <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/routing/managed-encryption#assign-role" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CMEK must have encrypt/decrypt access</a> granted to the KMS service account): <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">gcloud logging buckets update BUCKET_NAME --location=LOCATION --cmek-kms-key-name FULL_KMS_KEY_NAME</span></li>
</ul>
<p>Subsequently, the attacker can remove the permissions granted to the external key. At this point, the victim will be unable to read the logs, as the Google Cloud panel in Figure 6 shows.</p>
<figure id="attachment_182146" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182146" style="width: 792px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182146 size-full lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-351279-182090-6.png" alt="A screenshot of a Google Cloud log analysis interface showing an error message. The left panel displays &quot;Log fields data is unavailable because query is invalid.&quot; The main section shows a timeline graph with another message stating, &quot;Log histogram is unavailable because query is invalid.&quot; Below the graph, a section reads, &quot;Your input is invalid&quot; with zero results listed." width="792" height="262" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-351279-182090-6.png 792w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-351279-182090-6-786x260.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-351279-182090-6-768x254.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 792px) 100vw, 792px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182146" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 6. The outcome of an inaccessible encrypted key.</figcaption></figure>
<p>Any attempts to revert the key will result in the error message “rekeying requires that the CMEK service account has decrypt access to the current CMEK key,” as Figure 7 shows.</p>
<figure id="attachment_182157" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182157" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182157 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-353226-182090-7.png" alt="A screenshot of a terminal displaying an error message related to Google Cloud. The error indicates a failed precondition due to credentials issues with a Google service account regarding GKE keys." width="1000" height="101" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-353226-182090-7.png 2048w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-353226-182090-7-786x79.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-353226-182090-7-1920x194.png 1920w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-353226-182090-7-768x78.png 768w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-353226-182090-7-1536x155.png 1536w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182157" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 7. The outcome of an attempt to revert the key.</figcaption></figure>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_805ta0f3afvq"></a>Technique 5: Log Poisoning</h3>
<p>Another defense evasion technique is the direct modification of logs – known as log poisoning. This is an effective technique when logs are pre-configured to be written to a cloud storage resource. In this case, the logs are stored in JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) format and can be modified by an attacker. If stored logs are deleted, added or modified, there is a high likelihood that Security Operations Center (SOC) personnel or analysts would inadvertently use these poisoned logs to conduct log analysis.</p>
<ul>
<li>In AWS, CloudTrail logs are delivered as objects to an S3 bucket. An attacker with <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">s3:GetObject</span> and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">s3:PutObject</span> permissions on the bucket could download a log file, remove or alter specific events and then re-upload it, overwriting the original file. This breaks the chain of custody and invalidates the audit trail.</li>
<li>Figure 8 shows the response to a query from a scenario where an attacker alters a log to avoid detection, and then the victim inspects the log using <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/athena/latest/ug/what-is.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Amazon Athena</a>.</li>
</ul>
<figure id="attachment_182168" aria-describedby="caption-attachment-182168" style="width: 1000px" class="wp-caption alignnone"><img  class="wp-image-182168 lozad"  data-src="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-355229-182090-8.png" alt="A screenshot of response to a query from an attack scenario." width="1000" height="30" data-srcset="https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-355229-182090-8.png 1370w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-355229-182090-8-786x24.png 786w, https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/word-image-355229-182090-8-768x23.png 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption id="caption-attachment-182168" class="wp-caption-text">Figure 8. Athena query analysis shows the modified log.</figcaption></figure>
<ul>
<li>In Google Cloud, sinks route the logs to cloud storage. An attacker with <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">storage.objects.get</span> and <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">storage.objects.create</span> permissions can perform the same download and overwrite technique.</li>
</ul>
<p>To mitigate the risk of log poisoning, AWS provides <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">CloudTrail log file integrity validation</a>. This feature provides the ability to cryptographically verify whether log files were modified after they were delivered by CloudTrail. This ability is enabled by default when using the AWS Console to create Trails, but not when using the API or command line interface (CLI).</p>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_ejakm2tcga9"></a>Continuous Visibility</h2>
<p>Upon gaining an initial foothold in a victim environment, an attacker with advanced capabilities would aim to establish long-term, passive visibility into the victim's cloud infrastructure. Instead of running noisy discovery commands that might trigger alerts – or if they lack proper permissions – an attacker can target the log routing mechanism to route logs to their own environment, resulting in real-time visibility. This enables attackers to perform continuous discovery and passively monitor all activity, from new VM deployments and IAM policy changes to sensitive data access. In this way, attackers can map the environment, identify high-value targets, and escalate privileges while potentially remaining invisible to the victim's security monitoring. The following techniques achieve continuous visibility:</p>
<ol>
<li>Configure new log routing resource</li>
<li>Log redirection</li>
</ol>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_wm3o1wk4m886"></a>Technique 1: Configure New Log Routing Resource</h3>
<p>A direct method for achieving continuous visibility involves creating a new log routing resource – for example, an AWS trail or a Google Cloud sink. The attacker configures the newly created resource to direct logs to an external, attacker-controlled destination.</p>
<ul>
<li>In AWS, the attacker configures CloudTrail logging to their own S3 bucket by using the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">create-trail</span> API and specifying their bucket in the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">--s3-bucket-name</span> parameter.</li>
<li>In Google Cloud, the attacker utilizes the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">logging.sinks.create</span> API to set the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">DESTINATION</span> parameter to the attacker’s intended resource.</li>
</ul>
<p>Both of the above steps result in all logs being directed to the attacker's chosen destination.</p>
<p>For certain AWS accounts, the CreateTrail operation shows up in CloudTrail. If EventBridge is configured upon AWS account set-up, defenders can use EventBridge to alert on creation events. In this setup, subsequent describe calls of CloudTrail configuration will show the attacker's destination bucket. However, for organizations that use third parties or have not applied these configurations, attackers can carry out adversarial activities without being detected.</p>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_ar98i39izy5x"></a>Technique 2: Log Redirection</h3>
<p>Using this technique, the attacker alters the log routing destination to one within their own environment. This redirects logs to an attacker-controlled resource, enabling the attacker to obtain continuous discovery.</p>
<ul>
<li>In AWS, the attacker updates the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">--s3-bucket-name</span> parameter when invoking the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">update-trail</span> API. After modifying the destination bucket, all logs are directed to the attacker’s bucket, providing continuous discovery capabilities on the victim’s account.</li>
<li>In Google Cloud, the attacker uses <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">logging.sinks.update</span> permissions to update the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">destination</span> parameter, achieving the same ability to redirect logs.</li>
</ul>
<p>Small enterprises that manage their own alert telemetry may notice that Trails have stopped working in this situation, but larger organizations may not be using AWS-native services that would allow them to detect this behavior.</p>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_jk0pmy5epxx8"></a>Risk and Impact Assessment</h2>
<p>Table 1 summarizes the evasion and visibility techniques, the likelihood that the activity is malicious, and the impact on logging services.</p>

<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="width: 36.4135%; text-align: center;"><b>Technique Name</b></td>
<td style="width: 23.7877%; text-align: center;"><b>Likeliness of Malicious Activity</b></td>

</tr>

<p><span style="font-size: 10pt;">Table 1. Risk and impact assessment of evasion and visibility techniques.</span></p>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_av3biy3707u"></a>Prevention and Awareness</h2>
<p>The attack scenarios discussed all stem from modifications to logging service resources. Given the high value of cloud logging service resources, access should be restricted to highly privileged users to help prevent these scenarios. This measure reduces the likelihood of an attacker altering the configuration of such resources.</p>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_pgqqwt8f6e5u"></a>Amazon Web Services</h3>
<p>For every AWS account there is an immutable 90 day CloudTrail <a href="https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/view-cloudtrail-events.html" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Event History</a> of all management events. This fallback ensures that these records cannot be deleted or circumvented. However, data and network events do not appear in this history.</p>
<p>In AWS, limit the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">update-trail</span> API invocation to highly privileged users. Configure the bucket policy of the associated S3 bucket to prevent non-admin users from making configuration modifications. It's also crucial to ensure that only the CloudTrail service can write objects to these buckets.</p>
<h3><a id="post-182090-_juwdmanfmf1h"></a>Google Cloud</h3>
<p>Google Cloud provides a similar safety mechanism to AWS, through its <a href="https://docs.cloud.google.com/logging/docs/store-log-entries#system-created" target="_blank" rel="noopener">built-in log buckets</a>. The <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">_Required <span style="font-family: georgia, palatino, serif;">log</span></span> bucket serves as an immutable repository for essential logs – such as Admin Activity and System Event audit logs – that cannot be disabled, modified or deleted. Alongside this, the <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">_Default</span> log bucket automatically captures a broader range of log entries for a shorter period of time. When creating logging storage for external integration purposes, these built-in buckets will not be relevant. As a result, those manually configured buckets may remain exposed to the specific attack techniques described in this article.</p>
<p>In Google Cloud, restrict the permissions for <span style="font-family: 'courier new', courier, monospace;">logging.sinks.update</span>, and protect the destination resource.</p>
<h2><a id="post-182090-_oyq43tgh9bi2"></a>Conclusion</h2>
<p>Cloud logging services are fundamental for maintaining security posture and operational awareness, providing the definitive record of all activities within a cloud environment. The integrity of the logging infrastructure itself is a critical control, and for this reason has become a primary target for threat actors aiming to operate undetected.</p>
<p>The misuse of cloud logging services can have serious negative outcomes, enabling adversaries to cause blind spots for security teams, exfiltrate sensitive data in real-time, or methodically cover their tracks to evade forensics. By understanding the specific TTPs that threat actors use against these services, defenders can build more resilient detection and prevention strategies.</p>

</tr>
<tr style="height: 24px;">
<td style="width: 49.8596%; height: 24px;"><a href="https://docs-cortex.paloaltonetworks.com/r/Cortex-XDR/Cortex-XDR-Analytics-Alert-Reference-by-Alert-name/Suspicious-activity-on-logging-bucket" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Suspicious activity on logging bucket</a></td>
<td style="width: 125.983%; height: 24px;">Defense Evasion (TA0005)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p><span style="font-size: 10pt;">Table 2. Cortex alerts that indicate malicious activity in cloud logging services.</span></p>

 var PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE = 'en_US';

(function($) {
	// Migrated from the unit42-v5 + Modifications
	var subscribeSuccess = false;
	var email = document.getElementById('newsletter-email');
	var subscription_form = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form');
	var subscription_form_button = document.getElementById('unit42footerSubscription_form_button');
        var isCaptchaComplete02  = false;	
        window.captchaInlineFormOnload = function(token){
            isCaptchaComplete02 = true;
            $("form[name='Unit42_Subscribe'] button[id='unit42footerSubscription_form_button']").prop('disabled', false);
        }
        var PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = false;
        const SITE_KEY = '6LdDKhIsAAAAABdoYV3PR5VJ2Gz23_dLSvq2uvBQ'; 
                if(!PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED){
               PAN_INLINE_FORM_RECAPTCHA_LOADED = true;
               // trigger loading api.js (recaptcha.js) script
               var recapthaScript = $("script[src='https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload']").length
               // console.log("recapthaScript",recapthaScript);
               if (!recapthaScript) {
                   var head = document.getElementsByTagName('head')[0];
                   var script = document.createElement('script');
                   script.typerecapthaScript = 'text/javascript';
                   script.src = "https://www.google.com/recaptcha/enterprise.js?render="+SITE_KEY+"&hl="+PAN_LOAD_RECAPTCHA_LANGUAGE+"&onload=captchaInlineFormOnload";
                   head.appendChild(script);
               }
               else{
                   captchaInlineFormOnload();
                }
           }
            	
	
	$(subscription_form).submit(function(e) {
		e.preventDefault();
		e.stopImmediatePropagation();
		updateEmailMask();
		var success = true;
		var form = $(this);
		var mail = form.find('input[name="Email"]');
		
		if (mail.val() === '') {
			mail.addClass('has-error');
			showError(1);
			success = false;	
		}  else if (!isEmail(mail.val())){
			showError(2);
			success = false;
		}
		else {
			mail.removeClass('has-error');
			$('.error-mail').addClass('d-none');
		}

		

		if (success) {
                                                if(grecaptcha){
                        grecaptcha.enterprise.ready(function() {
                            grecaptcha.enterprise.execute(SITE_KEY, {action: 'submit'}).then(function(token) {
                                submitSubscribeForm({token :token, action : 'submit'},form);
                            });
                        });
                    }
                    			
		}
		return false;
	});
        function submitSubscribeForm(tokenData, form){
            var serialized_data = form.serialize();
            let captchaParams = `&g-recaptcha-response=${tokenData.token}&action=${tokenData.action}`;
            $.ajax({
				type: 'POST',
				url: form.attr('action'),
				data: serialized_data+captchaParams,
				beforeSend: function() {
                 form.find('button').addClass('is-loading');
    			},
				success: function(msg) {
					form.find('.form-success-message').html('<p class="success-message">You have been successfully subscribed</p>');
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					$(email).val('');
					clearError();
				},
				error: function(jqXHR, textStatus, errorThrown) {
					$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled', true);
					form.find('button').removeClass('is-loading');
					
				}
			});
            
        }
	function showError(error_type){
		if(error_type == 1) {
			$('.error-mail').text("Please enter the email address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		} else if(error_type == 2){
			$('.error-mail').text("Please provide a valid e-mail address.").addClass('error-show');
			$(subscription_form_button).addClass('is-disabled');
		}	
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
	}
	function clearError(){
		$('.error-mail').text("").removeClass('error-show');;
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-loading');
		$(subscription_form_button).removeClass('is-disabled');
	}
	
	$(email).on('input', function (event) { 
		var email = $(this).val();
		if (isEmail(email) ) {			
			clearError();
		} else if(email == ""){
			clearError();
		} else{
			showError(2);			  
		}
    });

	function isEmail(email) {
		var re = /^(([^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+(\.[^<>()\[\]\\.,;:\s@"]+)*)|(".+"))@((\[[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\.[0-9]{1,3}\])|(([a-zA-Z\-0-9]+\.)+[a-zA-Z]{2,}))$/;
		return re.test(String(email).toLowerCase());
	}
	
	
	
	function updateEmailMask() {
		var email = $("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='Email']").val();
		if (email && email.trim() != '') {
			var maskedEmail = maskEmailAddress(email);
			$("#unit42footerSubscription_form input[name='emailFormMask']").val(maskedEmail);
		}
	}

	function maskEmailAddress (emailAddress) {
		function mask(str) {
			var strLen = str.length;
			if (strLen > 4) {
				return str.substr(0, 1) + str.substr(1, strLen - 1).replace(/\w/g, '*') + str.substr(-1,1);
			}
			return str.replace(/\w/g, '*');
		}
		return emailAddress.replace(/([\w.]+)@([\w.]+)(\.[\w.]+)/g, function (m, p1, p2, p3) {
			return mask(p1) + '@' + mask(p2) + p3;
		});

		return emailAddress;
	}

}(jQuery));
//# sourceMappingURL=main.js.map
	
</script>
<!--  End: Footer subscription form -->

<script type="text/javascript">
	$(document).ready(function(){
		$("html").on("click", ".language-btn", function () {
			$(this).toggleClass("expand");
			$(".language-dropdown").toggleClass("expand");
		});

		$("html").on("click", "body", function (b) {
			if (!$(b.target).is(".language-btn")) {
				$(".language-btn").removeClass("expand");
				$(".language-dropdown").removeClass("expand");
			}
		});
	});
</script>

	var isProcessing = false; 
    function alter_ul_post_values(obj,post_id,ul_type){
	
		if (isProcessing)    
		return;  
		isProcessing = true;   
		var like_nonce = jQuery('#_wpnonce').val();
		jQuery(obj).find("span").html("..");
                jQuery.ajax({
                    type: "POST",
                    url: "https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/wp-content/plugins/like-dislike-counter-for-posts-pages-and-comments/ajax_counter.php",
                    data: "post_id="+post_id+"&up_type="+ul_type+"&ul_nonce="+like_nonce,
                    success: function(msg){
                            jQuery(obj).find("span").html(msg);
                            isProcessing = false; 
                            jQuery(obj).find('svg').children('path').attr('stroke','#0050FF');
                            jQuery(obj).removeClass('idc_ul_cont_not_liked idc_ul_cont_not_liked_inner');
                    }
 		});
	}

    event.preventDefault();
   if (( typeof OneTrust != 'undefined') &&  (!!OneTrust)) {
       OneTrust.ToggleInfoDisplay();
    }else{
      var href = event.target.getAttribute('href');

    }
}

function loadScript(url, defer){
    var script1 = document.createElement('script');
    script1.setAttribute('type', 'text/javascript');
    script1.setAttribute('src',url);
    if(defer == true){
        script1.setAttribute('defer','defer');
    }
    document.head.appendChild(script1);
}
function loadScript1(url, callback){

    var script = document.createElement("script")
    script.type = "text/javascript";
    if (script.readyState){  //IE
        script.onreadystatechange = function(){
            if (script.readyState == "loaded" || script.readyState == "complete"){
                script.onreadystatechange = null;
                callback();
            }
        };
    } else {  //Others
        script.onload = function(){
            callback();
        };
    }
    script.src = url;
    document.getElementsByTagName("head")[0].appendChild(script);
}
if(referer == "CloudCortex" || referer == "Prisma" || referer == "Cortex" || referer == "Sase" || referer == "Unit" || referer == "Ngfw" || referer == "Idira"){

    setTimeout(function(){
      loadScript(main_site_criticalTopBase, false);
      loadScript1(main_site_criticalTopProductNav, function(){
        window.PAN_initializeProduct2021Nav();
      });
      loadScript(main_site_defered, false);
    }, 3000);
	}

      loadScript1(main_site_critical_top, function(){
        window.PAN_initializeProduct2021Nav();
      });
      loadScript(main_site_defered, false);
    }, 3000);
	}
}

document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function() {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  // Loop through each form
  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];

    // Check if the hidden input field already exists
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (!requestInput) {
      // Create a hidden input element if it doesn't exist
      requestInput = document.createElement("input");
      requestInput.type = "hidden";
      requestInput.name = "web_unit42_req_id";
      requestInput.id = "web_unit42_req_id";

      // Append the hidden field to the form
      form.appendChild(requestInput);
    }
  }
});

// Assign the onCheqResponse function to the window object to handle events from any form
window.onCheqResponse = function(encryptedMessage, requestID) {
  // Find all the forms on the page
  var forms = document.getElementsByTagName("form");

  for (var i = 0; i < forms.length; i++) {
    var form = forms[i];
    var requestInput = form.querySelector("input[name='web_unit42_req_id']");
    if (requestInput) {
      requestInput.value = requestID;
    }
  }
};
